annotations.keyFindings: Across 26 trials, group visits lowered HbA1c by about 4.4 mmol/mol at 6 to 12 months, with larger effects in more intensive programmes and higher baseline HbA1c.
annotations.limitations: Substantial heterogeneity; few patient-reported outcomes; attendance inconsistently reported.

annotations.keyFindings: In 24 practices, group consultations gave an HbA1c difference of 2.1 mmol/mol with an interval crossing zero, better diabetes distress scores, and attendance at half the sessions by 61 percent.
annotations.limitations: Wide interval; full-time workers attended least.

annotations.keyFindings: Attenders had 6 mmol/mol lower HbA1c than non-attenders, but they were younger, more often retired and better controlled beforehand; adjustment shrank the difference to 2 mmol/mol.
Peer learning was valued; some patients disliked discussing results in front of neighbours; limited English and shift work hindered attendance.
Clinician time per patient was 28 percent lower with group visits, provided sessions were at least 70 percent full.
Individually randomised trials of group care often shared clinicians across arms and ignored clustering within groups, overstating precision.

claims.text: Across 26 randomised trials, group visits lowered HbA1c by a mean of 4.4 mmol/mol compared with individual care.
claims.passage: group visits lowered HbA1c by a mean of 4.4 mmol/mol (95 percent CI 2.7 to 6.1)
claims.interpretation: A plausible effect exists but is modest and varies between programmes.

claims.text: In a cluster-randomised trial in general practice, the HbA1c difference was 2.1 mmol/mol with an interval crossing zero, and only 61 percent attended half the sessions.
claims.passage: the mean difference in HbA1c was 2.1 mmol/mol in favour of group consultations (95 percent CI -0.6 to 4.8)
claims.interpretation: The effect in routine general practice is uncertain, which is the partners' question.

claims.text: Patients who attend group visits differ from non-attenders in age, retirement and baseline control, so records comparisons are confounded.
claims.passage: they were younger, more often retired and had better HbA1c before their first group visit
claims.interpretation: Comparing the practice's attenders with non-attenders would not answer the question.

claims.text: Some patients avoid group visits because of privacy, limited English or shift work.
claims.passage: People who spoke limited English and people with shift work found it hardest to take part.
claims.interpretation: An expansion could widen inequalities unless the trial measures who takes part.

synthesis: Six retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. Trials overall suggest group visits lower HbA1c modestly, but the most applicable general practice trial found a small effect with an interval crossing zero and incomplete attendance. Comparisons of attenders with non-attenders are confounded by who chooses to attend. Group visits may save clinician time when sessions are full, but patients with limited English or shift work take part least. Individually randomised trials of group care need partially nested analyses and attention to shared clinicians.
gradeRationale: Many randomised trials with a consistent direction for HbA1c, downgraded once for inconsistency; the applicable general practice trial is imprecise.
summary: Six retrieved records appraised; four source-derived claims; overall certainty moderate for HbA1c.
